promptText: What is the relationship between Spring Boot and the Spring Framework?
options: Spring Boot is a layer built on top of Spring that adds auto-configuration, starter dependencies, and an embedded server, without replacing Spring's IoC container
Spring Boot is a completely separate framework with its own IoC container that replaces Spring's
Spring Boot only works with reactive applications, unlike traditional Spring
Spring Boot removes the need for Spring's dependency injection mechanism entirely
explanation: Spring Boot bundles the same Spring modules (Core, MVC, Data, Security) with auto-configuration, curated starter dependencies, and an embedded server to reduce boilerplate; it uses the same Spring IoC container and DI mechanism under the hood rather than replacing either. It works for both servlet and reactive stacks, not exclusively reactive.

promptText: A team adds spring-boot-starter-data-jpa but the JDBC driver and JPA classes end up absent from the final classpath due to a build misconfiguration. What happens to the auto-configuration classes guarded by @ConditionalOnClass, and how does this differ from what @ConditionalOnMissingBean would do in the same situation?
options: @ConditionalOnClass causes the configuration to be silently skipped because the required classes aren't present; @ConditionalOnMissingBean instead checks whether a bean of that type already exists in the context, which is a completely different condition
Both annotations check the exact same condition (classpath presence), so the outcome would be identical either way
@ConditionalOnClass throws a startup exception listing the missing classes, while @ConditionalOnMissingBean silently skips
Neither annotation has any effect at build time; both are evaluated only when a bean is first requested at runtime, not at startup
explanation: @ConditionalOnClass activates a configuration only when specified classes are present on the classpath, and fails its condition silently (no exception) when they're absent; @ConditionalOnMissingBean is a fundamentally different check -- it looks at whether a bean of a given type already exists in the context, regardless of classpath contents. Both conditions are evaluated during context startup (bean definition registration), not lazily on first bean request.

promptText: What does @ConditionalOnMissingBean allow Spring Boot's auto-configuration to do, and why doesn't declaring your own DataSource bean cause a duplicate-bean conflict?
options: It only creates the default bean if the user hasn't already defined one of that type, so auto-configuration backs off automatically once a custom bean is declared
It always creates the default bean regardless of user configuration, and Spring silently discards whichever bean was registered second
It only applies when running in the 'dev' profile, so declaring a custom bean in 'prod' would still conflict
It merges the fields of the user's bean and the auto-configured default into a single combined bean instance
explanation: @ConditionalOnMissingBean lets auto-configuration supply a sensible default while backing off automatically the moment the developer defines their own bean of that type, which is exactly why declaring your own DataSource never conflicts with Boot's default. It is unrelated to active profiles, and there is no field-level merging between a custom bean and the skipped default -- the default configuration simply never runs.

promptText: What is the main benefit of Spring Boot starter dependencies like spring-boot-starter-web, beyond just saving a few lines in the build file?
options: They bundle a curated, version-compatible set of libraries for a capability, managed through Boot's parent POM/BOM, eliminating manual dependency-version conflicts
They replace the need for an embedded server, since starters run entirely without any HTTP server component
They automatically generate the application's business logic and controller classes
They disable auto-configuration for that feature, requiring you to configure everything by hand instead
explanation: Starters are tested bundles of dependencies (e.g., spring-boot-starter-web brings in Spring MVC, embedded Tomcat, Jackson, and validation) whose versions are governed by Boot's parent POM/BOM, eliminating the classic 'works on my machine' problem from mismatched transitive library versions. spring-boot-starter-web specifically brings the embedded server with it, and starters enable (not disable) the corresponding auto-configuration.

promptText: A team has many related settings under the 'app.mail' prefix (host, port, credentials) and is deciding between several @Value fields versus one @ConfigurationProperties class. Why is @ConfigurationProperties the better fit here specifically, beyond just 'grouping'?
options: It supports relaxed binding (mail-host/mailHost/MAIL_HOST all resolve to the same field) and Bean Validation on the bound object, neither of which @Value provides
@Value cannot read values from application.yml at all, only from application.properties files
@ConfigurationProperties is mandatory for Spring Boot to start; without at least one such class, the context fails to initialize
@Value only supports SpEL expressions and cannot read plain literal property values
explanation: @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole prefix into one strongly typed object with relaxed binding (mail-host/mailHost/MAIL_HOST all resolve) and supports attaching Bean Validation annotations so misconfiguration fails fast at startup -- capabilities @Value simply doesn't have. @Value reads plain properties from either file format just fine (SpEL is an additional capability, not its only mode), and @ConfigurationProperties classes are entirely optional, not required for startup.

promptText: A Docker image must run as either 'dev' or 'prod' depending on the environment, without being rebuilt. A developer hardcodes `spring.profiles.active=prod` inside application.yml before building the image, reasoning that it can always be overridden later. What's wrong with relying on this as the primary mechanism, and what should be used instead?
options: Baking the value into the packaged file means every deployment must remember to override it correctly; setting SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE as a runtime environment variable lets the same immutable image behave correctly per environment with no override discipline required
Nothing is wrong; a hardcoded value in application.yml already takes precedence over any environment variable, so overriding it later has no effect anyway
application.yml cannot contain a spring.profiles.active key at all; only command-line arguments are valid for setting it
The hardcoded value would cause the application to fail to start in any environment other than 'prod'
explanation: Setting SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE as an environment variable lets one immutable image behave differently per environment purely through runtime configuration, without depending on every deployment remembering to override a baked-in default. Environment variables take precedence over the value in the packaged application.yml (not the other way around), spring.profiles.active is a perfectly valid property key, and a 'wrong' profile value doesn't itself prevent startup.

promptText: By default, Spring Boot exposes only a minimal set of Actuator endpoints (mainly health) over HTTP. A security reviewer flags that /actuator/env and /actuator/heapdump are reachable in production, but the on-call engineer argues 'they can only be read by someone who already has network access to our internal tools, so it's not a real risk.' What's the strongest counter-argument grounded in what those endpoints actually expose?
options: /actuator/env can reveal configuration values (potentially including secrets), and /actuator/heapdump can dump the entire JVM heap, which may contain in-memory credentials or session data -- exposure risk exists independent of who else has network access, since access-control layers can themselves be misconfigured or bypassed
The engineer is correct; since network access is already restricted, exposing these endpoints publicly poses no additional risk
These two endpoints only return metrics like request counts and JVM uptime, so there is no sensitive data exposure concern at all
The risk is purely theoretical because Spring Boot encrypts all Actuator endpoint responses by default
explanation: /actuator/env and /actuator/heapdump can leak real configuration secrets and in-memory data (credentials, session tokens) respectively, so their exposure is a genuine risk that doesn't depend on trusting one particular network boundary -- defense in depth means not relying solely on network access controls that could themselves fail or be bypassed. These endpoints are far more sensitive than simple metrics/uptime data, and Spring Boot does not encrypt Actuator responses by default; that's why exposure is opt-in and typically paired with Spring Security and a separate management port.

promptText: Given the input string "   " (three spaces) on a field, which combination of Bean Validation annotations correctly describes its validation outcome, and why?
options: It passes @NotEmpty (length is greater than zero) but fails @NotBlank (which trims before checking, leaving an empty string)
It fails both @NotEmpty and @NotBlank, since both trim the string before checking
It passes both @NotEmpty and @NotBlank, since neither annotation considers whitespace-only content invalid
It fails @NotEmpty but passes @NotBlank, the reverse of the actual behavior
explanation: @NotEmpty only rejects null and zero-length values, and three spaces has length 3, so it passes; @NotBlank trims the string before checking and therefore rejects a whitespace-only string. @NotEmpty specifically does NOT trim before checking length, which is exactly why it's weaker than @NotBlank for validating required text fields like names and emails.

promptText: A team's @RestControllerAdvice class has separate @ExceptionHandler methods for UserNotFoundException (returns 404) and MethodArgumentNotValidException (returns 400), but no handler for a generic RuntimeException. What happens when an unexpected NullPointerException is thrown from a controller, and why is adding a catch-all handler for Exception.class generally recommended?
options: Without a matching handler, Spring's default error handling takes over and typically returns a generic 500 response (potentially with a default error page/body); adding a catch-all handler lets the team control the response shape and avoid leaking a stack trace
The request hangs indefinitely because @RestControllerAdvice cannot process an exception type it wasn't explicitly told about
Spring automatically maps any unhandled exception to a 404 Not Found response by default
The application crashes entirely and must be restarted, since no @ExceptionHandler matched
explanation: When no @ExceptionHandler matches, Spring Boot's default error-handling mechanism takes over and typically produces a generic error response (by default a 500 with Whitelabel Error Page content or a basic JSON body); adding a catch-all handler for Exception.class lets the team enforce their own consistent error contract instead of relying on that default. The request does not hang or crash the application, and unmatched exceptions default toward a 500-class response, not 404.

promptText: Why is `log.info("User {}", id)` preferred over `log.info("User " + id)` even when the log level is set to INFO and the statement will definitely be printed either way?
options: Beyond the performance benefit at suppressed levels, the parameterized form avoids string concatenation cost on every call and handles null arguments more gracefully than manual concatenation
There is no real difference once the statement is guaranteed to print; the two forms are functionally and performance-wise identical in that case
The parameterized form encrypts the logged value automatically, unlike string concatenation
String concatenation is invalid syntax inside a log.info() call and will not compile
explanation: Even when a statement is guaranteed to print, the parameterized {} form still avoids the minor overhead of manual string concatenation and handles a null id argument more predictably than string concatenation (which could throw or produce 'null' inconsistently depending on context); the bigger win, though, is that concatenation always builds the string even at a suppressed log level, while the {} form does not. Both forms compile fine syntactically, and neither encrypts anything.

promptText: In a multi-instance deployment (Instance A, B, C) each using its own local (in-JVM) cache for the same @Cacheable data, Instance A processes an update and calls @CacheEvict to clear its local entry. What correctness problem remains, and why doesn't @CacheEvict on Instance A solve it cluster-wide?
options: Instances B and C still serve their own stale cached values, because @CacheEvict only clears the cache within the JVM where it executes -- a local cache has no visibility into other instances' memory
There is no remaining problem; @CacheEvict automatically broadcasts the eviction to every instance in the cluster over the network
Instance A's update is rejected until all instances have separately confirmed the eviction
Local caches are inherently consistent across instances because the JVM shares heap memory across separate processes
explanation: A local cache lives entirely inside its own JVM's heap, so @CacheEvict executing on Instance A has zero effect on Instance B or C's private cache copies, which keep serving stale data until their own entries expire naturally. @CacheEvict does not broadcast across a cluster on its own (that requires a shared cache like Redis, where eviction is immediately visible to every instance since they all read from the same external store), and separate JVM processes do not share heap memory.

promptText: Inside a Spring bean, methodA() (not annotated) calls this.sendEmailAsync(), where sendEmailAsync() is annotated @Async. Separately, the team knows @Transactional suffers the identical self-invocation problem. What is the shared root cause, and would injecting the bean into itself (self-injection) and calling sendEmailAsync() through that injected reference fix it?
options: Both rely on a Spring AOP proxy wrapping the bean; a call through 'this' bypasses the proxy entirely, but calling through a self-injected reference (which IS the proxy) would restore the advice, fixing both cases identically
The two annotations have unrelated root causes; @Async fails due to thread-pool exhaustion while @Transactional fails due to isolation-level conflicts
Self-injection would not help in either case, since Spring always resolves 'this' to the proxy automatically regardless of how the reference was obtained
@Async and @Transactional only share this problem when the method being called is also marked private
explanation: Both @Async and @Transactional are implemented via a Spring AOP proxy; calling through 'this' from within the same object uses the raw target instance, never the proxy, so any proxy-based advice is skipped -- self-injecting the bean and calling through that injected reference does work as a fix, because the injected reference IS the proxy, not the raw object. The root causes are identical (proxy bypass), not separate mechanisms like thread-pool exhaustion or isolation conflicts, and the problem occurs regardless of whether the called method is private.

promptText: A scheduled job's execution time can vary widely (sometimes 2 seconds, sometimes 90 seconds) and it must never have two instances running concurrently. The job is currently configured with fixedRate = 30000. What specifically goes wrong, and which attribute fixes it?
options: fixedRate times the next start from the beginning of the previous run, so a 90-second execution causes overlapping runs; fixedDelay instead waits for the previous run to finish before starting the delay countdown, guaranteeing no overlap
Nothing goes wrong; fixedRate already guarantees no two executions ever run concurrently regardless of duration
The fix is to switch to a cron expression, since fixedRate and fixedDelay are both incapable of preventing overlap under any configuration
initialDelay should be used instead, since it is specifically designed to prevent concurrent executions of a recurring job
explanation: fixedRate measures the interval from the start of each execution, so if a run takes longer than the configured rate (90s > 30s here), the next execution's scheduled start time has already arrived before the previous one finished, causing overlap; fixedDelay instead measures the gap from the end of one execution to the start of the next, which guarantees runs never overlap regardless of duration. cron can also overlap if not paired with concurrency guards, and initialDelay only affects the first run's start time, not overlap between subsequent runs.

promptText: What problem does graceful shutdown (server.shutdown=graceful) solve during a Kubernetes rolling deployment, and what does it NOT solve on its own?
options: It allows in-flight requests to complete before the process exits, preventing dropped requests when a pod is terminated -- but it doesn't stop the load balancer from routing new traffic to a pod that's already shutting down unless coordinated with readiness probes
It guarantees the load balancer instantly stops sending traffic to a terminating pod with zero additional configuration required
It speeds up application startup time by skipping unnecessary auto-configuration steps during shutdown
It automatically retries any failed database migration that was running at the moment of shutdown
explanation: Graceful shutdown gives active, in-flight requests a bounded grace period to finish before the process actually exits, but the full picture requires coordinating with the orchestrator (a preStop hook and readiness probe) so the load balancer stops sending new traffic before the grace period begins -- graceful shutdown alone doesn't control the load balancer's routing decisions. It has no effect on startup speed (a separate concern entirely) or on database migrations.

promptText: A UserService publishes a UserCreatedEvent via ApplicationEventPublisher, and a listener sends a welcome email using @EventListener (no @Async). If the welcome-email listener throws an exception, and the publish happens inside a @Transactional service method, what is the default behavior, and how would @TransactionalEventListener change it?
options: By default, listeners run synchronously on the publisher's thread within the same transaction, so a listener exception can affect the publishing transaction; @TransactionalEventListener instead defers the listener until after the transaction successfully commits, decoupling listener failures from the transaction outcome
Listeners always run asynchronously on a separate thread by default, so a listener exception has no effect on the publisher's transaction regardless of annotation choice
@TransactionalEventListener is required for any listener to run at all; without it, @EventListener methods are silently never invoked
The listener exception is always swallowed silently by Spring's event mechanism, regardless of which annotation is used
explanation: Spring's plain @EventListener runs synchronously on the publisher's thread by default, meaning it participates in the same transaction, so an exception there can propagate back and affect the publishing transaction; @TransactionalEventListener instead defers invocation until after the transaction commits successfully, which decouples the listener's own failures from the original transaction's outcome. Plain @EventListener methods are invoked by default without needing @TransactionalEventListener, and exceptions are not silently swallowed by default in either case.
